source_notes.label: Polymer as growth medium and matrix
source_notes.summary: The authors grow PbS directly within MEH-PPV, using the polymer as a growth-controlling medium and continuous conductive matrix. They propose steric effects of the polymer chain, rather than charged surfactant groups, as the main growth-control mechanism. Polymer conformation and passivation are not measured atom by atom.
source_locators: Main PDF p. 1–2, Synthesis concept and growth discussion

source_notes.label: Structural scope of the composite
source_notes.summary: The cleaned material forms a continuous thin composite film containing nonaggregated, polydisperse PbS nanocrystals. The reported average size is4±2nm; the TEM aliquot harvest time is not separately stated. Cubic PbS is identified by selected-area diffraction along[111]. The2µm diffraction area is not a nanocrystal size.
source_locators: Main PDF p. 1–2, TEM discussion and Figure1

source_notes.label: Optical evidence and alternative explanations
source_notes.summary: Polymer emission decreases from the pre-injection reference through3- and15-minute samples. The authors interpret this as electronic coupling. They argue that the similar spectral shape accounts for reabsorption and that the lack of a free-ion absorption signature disfavors complex formation, while acknowledging dielectric changes could produce similar effects. No charge-transfer rate or absolute quantum yield is supplied.
source_locators: Main PDF p. 1–2, Figure2 and electronic-coupling discussion

source_notes.label: Boundaries of the lifetime and control evidence
source_notes.summary: The main cites ESI lifetime measurements as further support, but that ESI is not reviewed here. The authors also report bulk PbS without polymer; a separately specified recipe and quantitative control characterization are absent. Neither statement creates an invented additional synthesis–structure row.
source_locators: Main PDF p. 1–2, ESI footnote and polymer-free control discussion
